title: Visualising Ownership, Liability and Business Structures

visual_beats.directive: Build the ownership chart from a single owner node
Branch into incorporated and unincorporated forms
Reveal franchise, joint venture and public corporation nodes

narration.text: There are forms of business organisation. A sole trader is owned and controlled by one person. A partnership has two or more joint owners. A private limited company, or Ltd, has shareholders and limited liability. A public limited company, or Plc, can sell shares to the public. A franchise uses another firm's brand and system. A joint venture shares a project, and a public corporation is state-owned.

scenes.title: Sole Trader: Full Control, Unlimited Liability

visual_beats.directive: Show one owner locking the studio door
Draw a debt line straight into the personal savings jar
Stamp a red warning: no limited liability shield

narration.text: Rillstone Pottery is a sole trader: one owner controls the business and keeps all profit. Decisions are quick. But a sole trader has unlimited liability. The owner can be held responsible for business debts, so personal savings may be at risk. Capital is limited to the owner's own money. Because there is no separate legal identity, therefore limited liability never protects a sole trader.

visual_beats.directive: Add a second owner node to the org chart
Show both owners funding a second kiln
Send debt paths to both owners and display the agreement

narration.text: A partnership is formed when two or more people agree to jointly own a business. Fenwick and Rowe Ceramics brings extra capital and shared skills, so the studio can buy a second kiln. Partners usually share profit and decisions. Most partnerships still have unlimited liability, so each partner can be held responsible for debts. A partnership agreement sets out profit shares and responsibilities and is always recommended.

visual_beats.directive: Draw a legal shell around the company
Stop a debt line at the liability shield
Show shares passing only to private investors

narration.text: Larkspur Crafts Ltd is a private limited company. It has a separate legal identity, so the business itself can own assets. Shareholders enjoy limited liability: they are liable only for the amount they invested. Shares are sold privately to family, friends or specialist investors, not to the public. Because personal savings are protected, therefore owners risk only their investment. The trade-off is more paperwork and published accounts.

scenes.title: Public Limited Company: Plc
labels: Dividends and possible loss of control

visual_beats.directive: Expand the company block and fill a shareholder grid
Raise the capital bar
Lower the original owner control meter and show dividends

narration.text: Hearthside Goods Plc is a public limited company. Its shares can be sold to the public and are tradeable on the Stock Exchange. That raises far more capital for new sites and equipment. Shareholders still have limited liability. But the company must disclose more information, and original owners may lose control as new shareholders vote. Profits may be paid out as dividends to shareholders rather than kept for expansion. Growth brings scrutiny as well as funds.

scenes.title: Franchises and Joint Ventures
labels: Franchisee pays a fee for brand and system
Joint venture shares capital, risk and profit

visual_beats.directive: Stamp the outlet with the franchisor brand
Send a fee back to the franchisor
Join two separate firms on one shared project node

narration.text: Two other forms matter. Thornfield Market Goods is a franchise: the franchisee pays a fee to use an established brand, logos and trading methods. The franchisee gets support and a proven model, but follows rules and gives up independence. The franchisor expands with less capital. Kestrel and Vale Designs is a joint venture: two businesses share capital, risks and profits on one project while remaining separate.

scenes.title: Which Structure Suits a Growing Studio?
labels: Sole trader: control and all profit
Ltd: limited liability and shareholder funds

visual_beats.directive: Fill the sole trader panel with control icons then a red risk
Fill the Ltd panel with a shield and shareholder coins
Tilt the decision scale and hold both sides in view

narration.text: Which structure suits a growing craft studio? On the left, staying a sole trader keeps full control, all profit and simple decisions. However, unlimited liability puts personal savings at risk and capital stays small. On the right, becoming Larkspur Crafts Ltd gives limited liability and access to shareholder funds. The costs are higher administration and less privacy. Because growth needs capital, therefore the company form is safer, so the owner should weigh protection against paperwork.

scenes.title: Recap: Recommend a Business Structure
labels: Raise money for a third shop
Sole trader keeps control but full risk

elements.label: Craft retailer needs capital and protection

visual_beats.directive: Display the case facts and four options
Light the private limited company option
Raise the protected savings panel and the shareholder funds panel

narration.text: Apply the idea. A craft retailer wants two owners, limited personal risk and money to open a third shop. Should it remain unincorporated or become a company? A private limited company gives separate legal identity and limited liability, while shares stay private. A sole trader would keep control but face unlimited liability. Choose the structure, then watch the two balance panels move: personal savings protected on one side, shareholder funds added on the other.

recap_quiz.question: Two craft retailers want limited personal liability and to keep shares away from the public. Which structure suits them?
recap_quiz.visual_explanation: A liability shield appears around a company labelled Ltd while personal savings stay outside it; shares animate only to family and friends, and the Plc public-share grid stays greyed out.
